analysis.one_liner: Restores broad civil-rights protections under the ADA for workers and others with disabilities.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 402-17 on June 25, 2008, but the record shows no Senate vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: In the late 1990s the Supreme Court ruled that people whose conditions are controlled by medication or other measures often do not count as 'disabled' under the Americans with Disabilities Act, and courts had thrown out many discrimination cases on that basis. This bill rewrites the definition of disability so coverage is broad: a condition counts without regard to medication, prosthetics, or other measures that reduce its effects; conditions that come and go, like epilepsy or cancer in remission, count when active; and courts must read the definition in favor of broad coverage. It also bars job tests based on uncorrected vision unless they are job-related and a business necessity, and it leaves workers' compensation and disability benefit eligibility exactly as they are.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants with disabilities that the courts had screened out — including impairments managed with medication, hearing aids, prosthetics, or behavioral adaptations, and conditions like epilepsy, diabetes, or cancer that come and go. It also protects people who are discriminated against because of an impairment they are merely perceived to have.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates a broad definition of disability: whether an impairment substantially limits a major life activity is decided without regard to the ameliorative effects of medication, medical equipment, prosthetics, hearing devices, or reasonable accommodations, with a narrow exception for ordinary eyeglasses and contact lenses.

Counts impairments that are episodic or in remission as disabilities if they would substantially limit a major life activity when active, and lists major life activities to include concentrating, reading, sleeping, standing, and major bodily functions such as immune and neurological function.

Protects people who are subjected to a discriminatory action because of an actual or perceived impairment, whether or not it limits a major life activity, and instructs that the definition 'shall be construed broadly.'
Bars qualification standards, employment tests, or selection criteria based on uncorrected vision unless they are shown to be job-related and consistent with business necessity.

Directs the Attorney General, EEOC, and Secretary of Transportation to issue regulations implementing the new definitions, so the standard applies consistently across employment and public accommodations.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of all sizes, and businesses open to the public, face a much larger pool of people covered by the ADA, more requests for reasonable accommodation, and more exposure to discrimination lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: Broader coverage means more disability-discrimination claims and more accommodation obligations for employers, which is the business community's core objection to the bill's purpose.
People covered only under the 'regarded as' prong — those discriminated against for an impairment they do not actually have — are not entitled to a reasonable accommodation under the bill.
The effects of ordinary eyeglasses and contact lenses are still considered, so vision correctable with standard lenses generally does not count as a disability.

The bill explicitly does not change eligibility standards for state workers' compensation or federal and state disability benefit programs, so it restores courtroom protection without expanding anyone's benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain for workers with disabilities is large and direct: the Supreme Court decisions the bill overturns had let courts dismiss cases involving conditions like epilepsy, diabetes, and cancer in remission. The costs fall on employers in the form of broader liability and more accommodation duties, which is precisely what the bill is designed to impose; a good-faith objection is that 'regarded as' coverage without any accommodation duty and the eyeglasses exception are real limits, and the savings clause leaves benefit programs untouched. On balance the trade is one the House endorsed nearly unanimously.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House 402-17 and was placed on the Senate calendar in late June 2008, but the record shows no Senate vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 26, 2007 as the 'ADA Restoration Act of 2007' and referred to four House committees.

Congress wrote into the bill its finding that the Supreme Court's Sutton (1999) and Toyota (2002) decisions had narrowed ADA protection, eliminating coverage for many people Congress had intended to protect.

The House Education and Labor Committee ordered the bill reported 43-1 and the Judiciary Committee 27-0 on June 18, 2008, and both committees reported it amended on June 23; the Transportation and Energy and Commerce Committees were discharged.
On June 25, 2008 the House passed the bill 402-17, with 228 of 235 voting Democrats and 174 of 199 voting Republicans in favor.

The Senate received the bill, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on June 27, 2008; the provided record shows no further Senate action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing broader disability-discrimination exposure are better off if the bill stalled: the expanded pool of covered workers, the rule ignoring mitigating measures, and the bar on uncorrected-vision testing never took effect. Workers whose conditions are controlled by medication or are episodic lost their chance at restored protection.

for.name: House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a June 18, 2008 markup, ordered the bill reported 43-1, and reported it amended on June 23, 2008.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported 27-0 on June 18, 2008 and reported it amended on June 23, 2008.

for.name: F. James Sensenbrenner
for.role: Senior House Republican on the bill
for.what_they_did: Demanded a recorded yeas-and-nays vote on passage rather than voice vote.

for.name: Business and employer groups (including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce)
for.what_they_did: Opposed the original broader House proposal and pressed for the negotiated limits in the final version, including the eyeglasses exception and the workers' compensation savings clause.

against.name: 17 House Republicans
against.role: House Republicans voting no on passage

against.name: Business and employer groups (including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the original version of the bill as too expansive for employers before the final compromise was reached.

against.name: Senate (no recorded vote)
against.what_they_did: Placed the bill on the legislative calendar on June 27, 2008; the record shows no Senate vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The fight was not by party: 255 House members cosponsored (199 Democrats, 56 Republicans), the House passed it 402-17 with every voting Democrat in favor and 174 of 199 voting Republicans in favor, and both committees reported it with near-unanimous votes.

industries.note: The bill vastly expands who counts as disabled, so employers face more accommodation requests and more discrimination lawsuits; the bill's savings clauses cap some of that exposure but leave the core expansion intact. Its interest in limiting liability runs against the workers the bill protects.

industries.industry: Businesses open to the public (public accommodations)
industries.note: Broader coverage extends to discrimination in places of public accommodation, though entities need not provide accommodations to people covered solely because they are 'regarded as' having an impairment.
